mcqs.question: A candidate says a problem is 'in NP, so it must not have a polynomial-time algorithm.' What's wrong with this statement?
options: Nothing — that's exactly what NP means
NP means a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time; it does NOT mean the problem is hard to solve — every problem in P is also in NP
NP problems can never be verified in polynomial time
NP is only defined for problems with no known algorithm at all
mcqs.explanation: NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time, defined by fast verifiability of a proposed solution — not by the absence of a fast solving algorithm. In fact every problem solvable in polynomial time (P) is trivially also in NP, since you can just solve it and 'verify' by recomputing. Conflating NP with 'hard' or 'not polynomial' is one of the most common misconceptions in this topic.

mcqs.question: The halting problem is known to be NP-hard but is NOT NP-complete. Why not?
options: Because it's actually easier than every NP problem
Because it isn't in NP at all — it's not even decidable, so it can't satisfy the 'verifiable in polynomial time' requirement that NP-completeness needs
Because NP-hardness and NP-completeness are just two names for the same thing
Because the halting problem has never been proven to be at least as hard as every NP problem
mcqs.explanation: NP-complete requires both being NP-hard (every NP problem reduces to it) AND being a member of NP (verifiable in polynomial time). The halting problem satisfies the first (it's at least as hard as any NP problem) but fails the second — it's undecidable, so no algorithm can even always terminate to verify a proposed answer, let alone in polynomial time.
